name: Slendertone Face

card.summary: A consumer headset that sends electrical pulses to the facial muscles, marketed to tone and lift the face and soften the look of wrinkles.
card.note: Not for people with pacemakers or implanted devices, pregnancy, or certain heart conditions per trial exclusion criteria.

quick.overview:
Slendertone Face is a neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) device made by Bio-Medical Research, an Irish company. It is worn as a headset with electrode pairs placed on each side of the face over the facial nerve, just in front of the ear, and is marketed to tone facial muscles so the face looks firmer and more lifted.

The manufacturer registered a 2009 randomised trial of 108 women measuring the zygomaticus major muscle by ultrasound, but the registry entry reports no results. A separate 2024 split-face study of a different high-frequency facial NMES device in 24 Japanese women reported improvements in wrinkles, elasticity and jawline.
quick.how: Users wear the headset for a session of around 20 minutes, 5 days a week, which is the schedule used in the registered trial, and typically alongside their normal skincare. Results in studies are assessed over 6 to 12 weeks. Gel pads or conductive contact are used with such devices.
quick.risks: Trial exclusion criteria list pregnancy, implanted medical devices, heart disease, stroke, malignancy, insulin-dependent diabetes, facial surgery and Botox use, which indicates groups the manufacturer considered to need caution. Electrical stimulation devices can cause skin redness or discomfort at the pad sites.

lead: Slendertone Face is a headset-style electrical muscle stimulation device from Bio-Medical Research Ltd, designed for home use on the face. It delivers pulses through electrodes positioned on each side of the face over the facial nerve in front of the ear, causing facial muscles to contract [1].

The appearance idea is that regularly exercising facial muscles with stimulation can increase muscle tone and plumpness, giving a firmer, lifted look to the cheeks and jawline and a smoother skin surface. The manufacturer describes its goals as facial radiance, tone, lift, firmness and complexion [1].

Bio-Medical Research registered a randomised trial of the device in 2009. A 2024 study of a different high-frequency facial stimulation device reported improvements in wrinkles, sagging and elasticity in a small split-face trial [2].

angle.text: The headset is worn for about 20 minutes a day, 5 days a week, to tone facial muscles so the cheeks and jawline look firmer and lines look softer. Published results on this specific device are not available in the registry, and a related device study reported visible changes at 8 weeks.

infobox: Both sides of face over the facial nerve

paras: The device uses neuromuscular electrical stimulation, in which electrical pulses delivered through the skin trigger muscle contractions. In the registered trial, electrode pairs sat on each side of the face over the facial nerve, just in front of the ear [1]. The idea parallels body-toning stimulators sold under the Slendertone name, applied to the face.

Users wear the device regularly to firm the face. In the trial, the treated group used it 20 minutes a day, 5 days a week for 12 weeks while continuing usual routines and avoiding anti-ageing products, and the control group received no stimulation [1]. Manufacturer marketing cited by retailers reports increases in muscle plumpness and high self-reported firmness, but these figures come from the company rather than a published paper.

The registered study measured the zygomaticus major muscle by ultrasound at baseline and weeks 6 and 12, along with questionnaires on radiance, tone, lift, firmness and complexion; the registry entry lists no efficacy results, and enrollment (108) differs from the planned 100 [1]. Because the ultrasound endpoint measures muscle rather than wrinkle depth, the registry does not itself show a wrinkle outcome.

The registered 2009 trial (NCT01030380) was a two-group study of healthy women with visible facial ageing signs, sponsored by Bio-Medical Research; no results are reported in the registry entry [1]. A prospective split-face trial at a Tokyo hospital in 2023 enrolled 24 women aged 30 to 59 and tested a different high-frequency facial NMES device for 8 weeks; it reported significant improvements in wrinkles, elasticity, jawline angle, submental and cheek volume, nasolabial folds and blood flow compared with the untreated side, and the authors noted further studies are needed [2]. These results apply to that device, not to Slendertone Face.
The trial excluded pregnant participants and people with implanted medical devices, heart disease, stroke, malignancy, insulin-dependent diabetes, facial surgery or botulinum toxin use [1].

timeline.event: Bio-Medical Research runs a 12-week randomised trial of Slendertone Face (NCT01030380) [1].
Split-face study of a different high-frequency facial NMES device published [2].
